title: Bigger barns (Luke 12:13–21)
hookLine: a rich man plans his retirement and dies that night

lines: TELL MY BROTHER TO SPLIT IT.
cards: It starts with a family fight. Someone in the crowd shouts at Jesus: Master, tell my brother to split the inheritance with me. It's the tone of siblings across a lawyer's table after a funeral.
Jesus won't be the judge. Who made me a divider over you? He turns to the crowd: beware of all covetousness, because a man's life does not consist in the abundance of things he possesses.
Then he tells a story about a farmer whose year went very, very well.

teach.h: A HARVEST WITH NOWHERE TO GO.
teach.b: A rich man's land brings in a huge harvest, and he has nowhere to put it all. So he talks to himself, and Luke lets us listen. What shall I do?
I know. I will pull down my barns and build greater, and store everything there. And I'll say to my soul: soul, you have plenty laid up for many years, take your rest, eat, drink, enjoy yourself.

teach.h: MY CROPS, MY BARNS, MY SOUL.
teach.b: My crops, my barns, my goods, my soul. Nobody else is in the room: not his workers, not his neighbors, not the hungry, not God.
Then God speaks into the room: "Thou fool, this night do they require thy soul of thee: and whose shall those things be which thou hast provided?" He planned a retirement and didn't get an evening.
And the question cuts back to the brothers at the start: whose will it all be?
Jesus finishes: so is he that lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God. He isn't a fool for having a good harvest or for planning ahead. Joseph stored grain in Egypt and saved lives.
He's a fool because the harvest only ever went into barns.

teach.h: BASIL: THE EXTRA BREAD IS THEIRS.
teach.b: Saint Basil the Great, preaching on this parable, put it bluntly: the extra bread you store belongs to the hungry, and the shoes rotting in your closet belong to someone barefoot.
The Catechism calls this the universal destination of goods: what we own is meant, in the end, to serve everyone.

how: Catholics hear the parable of the rich fool at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel, and Catholic social teaching speaks of the universal destination of goods: private property is real, but its use is meant to serve the common good.

games.q: you're the farmer. your harvest is too big for your barns. what do you do?
o: tear them down and build bigger ones for yourself.
share the surplus with the village.
sell it all and buy more land.
games.why: he builds bigger barns and plans years of ease. God says: this night your soul is required of thee.

practice: Picture your own barns: a garage, a shelf, a savings account, a pile kept for someday, and walk through them slowly in your mind.
Notice one thing you aren't using that somebody else could: a set of tools, a sum of money, an hour you could give. If you pray, ask to be rich toward God.

wordCard.voice: Bigger barns. The rich farmer's plan to store everything for himself, and God's answer: this night your soul is required of you. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: fool, literally without understanding, one who doesn't think clearly about what matters.

carryVoice: Your line: this night. Not many years from now, but this very evening. Until tomorrow.
